§9.5.4 Repeated Identical Values

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

tables-repeated-identical-values · tables rowspan failure-mode

✅ Normative

A rowspan MUST be used only where the page genuinely merged the cell. A value printed k times at k distinct vertical positions MUST be rendered as k cells; repeated content MUST NOT be merged.

"82.13%" printed nine separate times, "Data Page" repeated down a column, the same rate on every row — the temptation is to collapse them into one spanning cell. That output is non-conforming.

Printed (9 separate lines):    Non-conforming output:
| 1 | 82.13% |                 | 1 | [rowspan=9]82.13%  |
| 2 | 82.13% |                 | 2 | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE  |  ← merges a value
| … | 82.13% |                 | … | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE  |    printed 9 times

Why merging is wrong, not just different

A rowspan is a claim about the page: "these cells are one cell." When the page printed nine cells, that claim is false — the never invent failure. Anyone counting records downstream then gets one where the document has nine, and the loss is invisible because the output still looks well-formed. A span that cannot be pointed to on the page is an error even when the values under it are right.

Deciding from the geometry

The decision MUST be taken from where the value is printed, not from how the column reads:

  • one printed occurrence spanning several rows → one cell with a rowspan;
  • distinct vertical positions → separate cells, one per row.

A column of identical values is exactly where the eye stops resolving lines, so the word positions on the page, not an impression of the column, settle it (see Boxes and Granularity§3.3). For the opposite case — where the page really did merge a cell across a multi-line record — see Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells§9.5.3.
